title: Public attention converges on economic security but diverges toward work, governance, or safety according to place and stability
source_unit: Gallup and World Governments Summit, The World's Most Important Problem: What People Need Leaders to Hear in 2026
geography: 107 countries and territories; regional, World Bank income-group, and conflict/stability comparisons

observations.period: 2025 fieldwork reported in 2026; global hierarchy of national problems

denominator.unit: countries and territories in Gallup World Poll analysis

economy.value: a median 23% of adults name the economy, living standards, prices, or wages as their country's most important problem

work.value: 10% name work or employment, 8% politics/government, and 7% safety/security; together with economic concerns these four categories account for roughly half of responses

secondary.value: food and shelter, social issues, environment and climate, and health each receive a median of 3%; education 2%, immigration 1%, infrastructure 1%, and media less than 1%

boundary.value: these are perceived national priorities, not objective rankings of harm, causal explanations, or individual life histories

observations.method: Gallup World Poll nationally representative probability-based adult samples collected by telephone or face-to-face in 107 countries and territories between March and October 2025; approximately 1,000 or more respondents per country or territory.
observations.uncertainty: Country medians compress different question contexts and category coding; sampling error, wording, nonresponse, and field conditions can affect comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Adults aged 15 and older, with published comparisons by region, World Bank income group, age, gender, life evaluation, household income perception, and conflict or stability context.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower-ranked issue may still be severe but displaced in public attention by more immediate economic, work, political, or security concerns.

observations.period: 2025 fieldwork reported in 2026; income, household room, and economic perception

denominator.unit: countries and territories compared by World Bank income grouping

income_gradient.value: people in lower-income countries more often name economic issues or affording basic needs, while 81% of people in low-income countries identify one of economy, politics, work, safety, or food/shelter among the five major themes versus 65% in high-income countries
income_gradient.unit: country-level adult survey medians by income group

lived_economy.value: people's feelings about household income are more closely related to naming the economy as the top national issue than GDP growth rates

youth.value: 34% of adults aged 15 to 34 name the economy or affording basic necessities as the top national concern, compared with 30% among adults 55 and older
youth.unit: adult survey estimate across analyzed countries

analytic_signal.value: public economic judgment is mediated by household room and felt security, not only by aggregate growth

observations.method: Gallup aggregate analysis of cross-country survey responses and reported relationships with perceived household income, GDP growth, age, and country income group.
observations.uncertainty: The reported relationships are descriptive and do not establish that income perception or GDP causes issue prioritization.
observations.subgroup: Young adults, older adults, women, lower-income households, people with poor life evaluations, and populations in lower-income countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Economic concern can reflect media salience, political framing, recent shocks, or expectations rather than only material shortfall.

observations.period: 2025 fieldwork reported in 2026; governance, trust, and local delivery

denominator.unit: countries and territories in institutional-trust and national-problem analysis

politics.value: politics and government are named as the top national problem by a median 8% globally, with higher concern in high-income countries and Northern America, Europe, and Latin America and the Caribbean

trust_gap.value: adults expressing confidence in none or one of five institutions are roughly twice as likely to name politics as the top problem as those confident in four or five institutions: 15% versus 8%
trust_gap.unit: estimated marginal means from aggregate cross-country analysis

local_route.value: Gallup identifies local conditions and services such as housing, healthcare, and education as strongly related to institutional confidence

analytic_signal.value: political legitimacy is judged through visible institutional performance and everyday service conditions, not only through national ideology or macro indicators

observations.method: Gallup cross-country survey analysis using institutional-confidence measures and regression-adjusted aggregate comparisons.
observations.uncertainty: The relationship between trust, service conditions, and political concern is associative; the report does not identify causal direction or specific institutional reforms that would change it.
observations.subgroup: Adults across income groups, residents of high-income democracies, local service users, and people with varying confidence in government, courts, elections, military, and financial institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher political concern in affluent democracies may partly reflect greater openness to criticism rather than only institutional failure.

observations.period: 2025 fieldwork reported in 2026; conflict, security, and attention displacement

denominator.unit: countries and territories compared by safety and security concern

conflict_priority.value: in countries experiencing violent conflict or instability, physical safety and security dominate public concern and can marginalize economic and political issues

examples.value: safety/security is named by 83% in Ukraine, 71% in Israel, and 55% in the State of Palestine in the report's country comparisons
examples.unit: adult survey estimates in selected countries and territories

peace_interaction.value: the report finds a strong relationship between objective peace measures and public concern about physical safety, while some countries show economic hardship displacing security concern

open_test.value: join price and household room, work quality, local service performance, trust, conflict exposure, media attention, safety experience, and later political response without treating public priority as a direct measure of objective risk

observations.method: Gallup survey analysis compared with Institute for Economics & Peace Global Peace Index measures and country context.
observations.uncertainty: Security salience is shaped by conflict, crime, economic hardship, recent shocks, and political communication; cross-country association is not causal proof.
observations.subgroup: Conflict-affected populations, residents of peaceful countries facing sudden violence, adults across age and gender, and populations experiencing severe economic hardship.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low reported security concern does not mean low insecurity; economic, political, or normalized violence can crowd out explicit security reporting.

related_sources.claim: The official Gallup report page provides the aggregate problem categories, regional and income patterns, institutional-trust analysis, conflict examples, and methodology.
Gallup's related analysis supplies complementary detail on global economic anxiety and household perceptions.
Institute for Economics & Peace peace measures provide the comparative security context referenced by Gallup.

boundary: This record adds an aggregate public-attention route from household economic security, work, service performance, institutional trust, and conflict exposure through perceived national problems and political judgment. It uses country-level survey aggregates and contextual comparisons, not respondent-level records, individual panel histories, causal effects, or a claim that perceived priority equals objective severity.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Gallup 2026 report page was reviewed for global category medians, regional and income differences, household economic perception, institutional trust, local service route, conflict/security displacement, selected country examples, and survey methodology.
